Liu et al.’s released implementation uses modified Fisher–Yates, not unrestricted permutation followed by rejection. Keep each user’s timestamp slots fixed; compute each item’s minimum timestamp across training interactions; freeze every occurrence whose timestamp equals that minimum. Scan positions i chronologically, choosing uniformly among unfrozen j≥i satisfying both availability inequalities: first(item_j)≤timestamp_i and first(item_i)≤timestamp_j; swap item IDs. Self-swaps are allowed. Required inputs: aligned user/item/event timestamps and cross-user training first observations; sequence positions alone are insufficient. The constrained routine uses global Python randomness, which the script’s --seed argument does not initialize. [Author code](https://github.com/yangl-iml/disentangle_sequential_patterns/blob/main/data_preprocessing.py)

Repeated items remain separate occurrences: multiplicities are preserved, without deduplication inside the shuffle. Timestamp equality is allowed; all occurrences at an item’s minimum timestamp are frozen, including ties across users. Sorting supplies no explicit semantic tie-break. The script splits first, shuffles complete training histories, and leaves validation/test interactions unchanged; it provides no special handling for truncated model windows. Its availability estimate is explicitly training-only, not a release date or full-dataset minimum. [Author code](https://github.com/yangl-iml/disentangle_sequential_patterns/blob/main/data_preprocessing.py)

Implementation implications/inference: compute minima before model-window truncation and retain timestamp alignment; shuffling only retained windows defines a different intervention. Training first observations can occur later than true availability, overconstraining permutations. Frozen events, narrow eligibility sets, repeats and ties leave residual order; the swap procedure does not establish uniform sampling over feasible permutations. Compare original/random/constrained performance alongside actual displacement and eligible-swap rates. Differences measure sensitivity to these perturbations, not causally isolated user preferences: popularity drift, seasonality, exposure, recency and global timeline leakage can remain. The paper’s stated goal is distinguishing availability-associated and behavioral sequence patterns, not identifying simulator diversity/conformity traits. [Paper abstract](https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/disentangling-user-and-item-sequence-patterns-in-sequential-recom/)
